support_quote: Participants with and without a visual impairment were recruited consecutively from the Waterloo Optometry and Vision Science (WOVS) Primary Care (general care), Ocular Health (ocular disease management) and Low Vision (vision rehabilitation) Clinics by a research assistant.
notes: q1 Y: 'recruited consecutively' is stated, but the sample was 'deliberately enriched' from Ocular Health and Low Vision clinics (not whole-population). q2 U: all participants came from the same university clinics (not a two-gate design), but enrichment is a milder form of spectrum selection. q3 U: adults over 65 who could speak English only; 4 of 93 excluded after enrolment (1 declined TICS-M, 2 did not complete the questionnaire, 1 declined all questions); people with cognitive impairment were kept in and analysed separately. q4 Y: enrolment was by clinic and recent exam, not by answers; this is the assessor's reading of the design, and no sentence states independence outright. Applicability High: over-65s only, enriched clinic sample, and the tool targets visual risk for falls for non-eye professionals, not LVR need. Left at Unclear, not Low, because of the enrichment.

support_quote: Aside from the preliminary questions A–C, all questions required a yes/no response.
notes: q1 U: the questionnaire was given by telephone up to 4 months after the eye exam. The text does not say whether interviewers or participants knew the exam results, and it does not say who scored the answers. q2 Y: each item is binary yes/no (item 5 is reversed) and the aggregate rule is 'yes to any question'; no cut-off was tuned. q3 U: items were compiled from existing questionnaires (VFQ-25 / Desmond / Saskatoon / Independent Mobility Questionnaire) and not selected from a larger pool by accuracy; the item-to-impairment-group mapping appears to be set by design, but this is not stated as pre-specified, and the TICS-M>21 subgroup looks post hoc. The same sample was used for development and validation, and the authors call the study 'preliminary'. q4 U: the same telephone script was used for everyone, but the interview was by phone, not by the non-eye health professionals who are the intended users. Applicability Low: 7 brief yes/no items prefaced 'with your glasses on', matching the review's target (brief self-report); the published wording is the wording that would be used.

support_quote: A retrospective chart review was then conducted.
notes: q1 U: the reference is best-corrected VA / contrast sensitivity / Amsler / confrontation fields or perimetry, but the target is a composite 'visual impairment as a fall risk' and the field and central-defect criteria are weak. q2 Y: the exam preceded the telephone interview and the chart review followed it, so the exam findings were recorded before the answers existed; blinding is not stated and this is inferred from the sequence. q3 U: the thresholds are stated but inconsistent: the text says VA '< 0.1 logMAR (<20/25)' while the Table 1 footnote says 'VA > 0.1 logMAR'; CS < 1.4; asymmetry > 0.1 logMAR. They do not appear pre-specified. q4 N: data were pulled retrospectively from clinical charts, with no study protocol for chart, distance or eye, and the abstract says 'various visual impairments'. High is kept because of q4 and the mild thresholds, which are not conventional low-vision cut-offs. Applicability High: the target is fall-related impairment (VA better than 0.2 logMAR may count, asymmetry, peripheral field) and not need for LVR.

support_quote: The participants had had a full eye exam at WOVS within the previous four months.
notes: q1 U: the interval is 'within four months' (slightly over the ~3-month benchmark) and no mention of cataract surgery or progression in the interval. q2 U: all participants had a chart-based reference, but it is not stated that every participant had every test (CS / fields / stereo); the number of tests per person is unclear. q3 Y: all participants were classified from the same type of source (the WOVS chart review). q4 Y: 93 enrolled and 89 analysed, with reasons given for the 4 exclusions; all 2x2 tables use the same 89 (Group 1: 31+58 = 89). Inconsistency: the abstract says '53 ... and 33' (=86) participants but the Results say 89. Judgement Unclear because of q1 and q2; the abstract/results count mismatch also lowers confidence. Possible overlap of the same participants across groups: the same people are analysed in more than one group.

support_quote: Among subjects in the Montreal area not eligible for other components of the CSHA, all positive subjects, along with a random sample of negative subjects, were selected to undergo a visual examination at home.
notes: q1 Y for stage 1 (random community sample of 1800 aged 65+, 1777 completed) but the 2x2 subsample was drawn only from Montreal-area people 'not eligible for other components of the CSHA' - I scored Y on the stage-1 frame; the subsample's representativeness is unclear. q2 Y: single community source, no two-gate design. q3 U: no explicit exclusions stated, but only 45.1% of eligible people were examined (handled in D4 q2); cognition/language exclusions not described. q4 N: verification enrolment depended on the screening answer (all positives + random sample of negatives); authors state 'the sensitivity and specificity estimated in this study cannot be applied to an unselected population'. I escalated this partial-verification sampling in D1 only; D4 q2 is scored on the participation loss alone. Applicability Low: community adults but 65+ only (not 18+), which I did not treat as a high concern.

support_quote: A visual disability was considered to be present if the answer to at least one of the following two questions was positive:
notes: q1 Y: questions asked at the stage-1 home interview before the stage-2 exam; no scorer involved. Judgement call: sequence is inferred from the two-stage design, and exam selection depended on the answers. q2 Y: threshold ('at least one yes') is the HALS/Statistics Canada definition, pre-existing. Caveat: four test criteria (near, distance, either, both) were all evaluated and reported, none chosen as best, but no primary criterion was pre-specified. q3 NA: no item selection from a pool. q4 Y: same two items and wording, home interview, for everyone, embedded in the larger CSHA survey (context differs from stand-alone clinic use). Applicability Low: brief 2-item screen for self-reported trouble with reading and distance vision; it targets visual disability rather than 'need for LVR' explicitly - judgement call.

support_quote: Distance VA was measured at 4 m using the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Survey charts17 in a back-lighted box.
notes: q1 Y: ETDRS chart, presenting and best-corrected VA, ICD-9 categories. q2 Y: 'The first author (JG), an optometrist who was not aware of the subjects' questionnaire responses at the time of the examination, carried out the visual assessment.' q3 Y: thresholds stated (mild 6/12, moderate 6/21, severe <=6/60 or field <20 deg), but four diagnostic definitions were reported, so no single primary one was pre-specified - judgement call, kept Y. q4 Y: study-specific protocol (4 m distance, 0.4 m near, eye, correction stated). Applicability Low: moderate impairment (VA <=6/21) matches Quebec rehabilitation eligibility; the 2x2 definitions use VA only (near OR distance), field loss is not part of them; the sample is a single examiner, which is a minor point.

support_quote: The final participation rate was 45.1%, 40.4% among those with a positive questionnaire and 47.4% among those with a negative questionnaire.
notes: q1 U: interval between the stage-1 interview (CSHA, 1991-92) and the home exam is not stated ('unable to schedule an eye examination before the end of the study'). q2 N: of 144 eligible, 31 lost to follow-up, 42 refused, 6 not scheduled; 65 examined (45.1%), well above the 20% loss threshold; non-participants did not differ on age or disability status but were more often women (62% vs 41%). q3 Y: all examined people received the same exam. q4 U: the 2x2 uses the 65 examined (19 positive, 46 negative); missing data are explained, but only 65 of 144 eligible are analysed - scored U to avoid double counting q2. High is by rule (q2 N), no downgrade.

support_quote: The recruitment aimed to include individuals across a broad spectrum of visual function; the measured binocular VA for this cohort ranged from −0.3 to 2.0 logMAR (mean ± SD, 0.58 ± 0.44 logMAR).
notes: q1 U: four US institutions, Jun 2019-Feb 2022, but no statement of consecutive/random/whole-population enrolment. q2 U: purposive 'broad spectrum' sampling (milder two-gate form per tailored rule); recruitment source not stated. q3 U: inclusion required age >=18, available VA and ability to communicate in English (survey is English-only); full inclusion/exclusion criteria deferred to the earlier survey paper (ref 7), which I was told not to read. Not scored N because English is intrinsic to an English item bank; if reviewer scores N, domain becomes High. q4 Y: all 385 analysed; no two-stage or answer-dependent verification. RoB Unclear: no N, but q1-q3 unreported. Applicability High: 68.6% had VA worse than 0.3 logMAR; authors state 'fewer normally sighted individuals than the general population' (p8); AMD 19.2%, glaucoma 16.9%; sample skewed to impaired people, so target prevalence is not representative of general screening.

support_quote: Third, the performance metrics reported here are based on responses collected within the context of the full 100-item survey.
notes: q1 U: order of survey versus VA measurement and blinding not described in this article (may be in ref 7). q2 Y: classification rule fixed a priori: 'no' = positive; for pairs/triplets 'no' to all items = positive; yes/no items so no cut-off tuning. q3 N: items, pairs and triplets chosen by ranking AUC over all 100 items (top 20 singles, 1980 pairs, then triplets) in the same 385-person sample, with no separate development or validation sample; authors call for external validation, so headline accuracies (Q97 AUC 0.85; Q30 AUC 0.80) are optimistic. q4 N: items answered inside the 100-item survey, not stand-alone (authors' limitation 3). High by rule (q3, q4 N). Applicability High: embedded in a 100-item battery; US-specific wording (fast-food menus, computer keyboard); stand-alone performance untested. Also: 5 items had suboptimal IRT fit (p3); AUC is the mean of sensitivity and specificity at a single threshold, not a true ROC AUC (note for synthesis, not a domain judgement).

support_quote: VA with habitual correction was assessed using standardized charts (Bailey–Lovie, ETDRS, or Snellen).
notes: q1 Y: measured VA with standard charts; correction status stated (habitual). q2 U: examiner blinding to survey answers not reported here. q3 Y: thresholds stated: 0.3 logMAR (20/40) low vision; 1.0 logMAR (20/200) VA-defined legal blindness. q4 U: charts varied (Bailey-Lovie/ETDRS/Snellen); binocular VA used when available, otherwise better-eye monocular; full protocol (distance etc.) deferred to ref 7, so not scored Yes (not N because 'standardized' charts were stated). Applicability Low: VA-defined low vision at a conventional threshold is an accepted proxy under the review protocol. Caveats: habitual-correction VA used whereas the stated clinical definition is best-corrected VA in the better eye (p1); binocular VA used; visual field, contrast and reading performance ignored (authors' limitation 1, p8). Ocular diagnoses came from physician notes plus self-report (recall bias), but diagnosis is not the reference standard.

support_quote: This analysis included 385 participants from a cohort described previously.
notes: q1 U: interval between survey and VA measurement not stated here; no mention of intervening surgery or LVR. q2 Y: having available VA data was an inclusion criterion, so all analysed participants had a reference standard independent of the answers; no partial verification mentioned. q3 U: all had VA, but via different charts and binocular versus better-eye monocular VA; same type of reference standard, but not scored Yes given the variation. q4 Y: 385 analysed with the same n across items; no dropouts or missing data reported (whether anyone was enrolled and then excluded would be in ref 7). Unclear overall because of q1 and q3; no N answers.

support_quote: A total of 365 consecutive patients participated in the study in order to replicate the original work of Wolffsohn and Cochrane.
notes: q1 Y on the authors' word 'consecutive'; no enrolment flow or screened-but-not-enrolled counts, and groups were then filled by VA criteria (170 impaired, 195 healthy), so this could equally be U. q2 N: two-gate design, with impaired patients (VA <=0.30 or 0.52 logMAR) and healthy controls (VA >=0.10 logMAR) both selected by VA; control group was younger (68.7 vs 78.8 y) and better educated; the VA gap between 0.10 and 0.30 was excluded (spectrum bias). q3 U: only stable-VA (<0.1 logMAR change in 6 mo) requirement stated; no other exclusions reported either way. q4 Y: enrolment was by VA and not by questionnaire answer. High RoB rests on q2. Applicability High: hospital/clinic ophthalmology patients vs healthy controls, not an LVR-need screening population; target is VA-defined impairment, mean age differs between groups.

support_quote: ROC analysis revealed a cut-off score of 105 or 106 as optimal for the classification of visually impaired patients and healthy subjects, with a sensitivity of 95.4% and a specificity of 91.8%.
notes: q1 U: patients had examination and questionnaire but order and blinding to VA are not stated. q2 N: cut-off chosen by ROC as optimal in the same sample, no pre-specification. q3 N: no separate derivation/validation sample (cut-off 105 or 106 tied, unvalidated). q4 N: mode differed by site (public hospital: three questionnaires by telephone interview in random order; private clinic: SLVQOL alone face-to-face); also the cut-off pools both. Applicability Unclear: the index test is the 25-item Spanish LVQOL (a full-length quality-of-life PROM, not a brief screening item), used to separate impaired from healthy rather than to flag LVR need.

support_quote: Patients with visual impairment were included in the study if their best-corrected distance visual acuity in the best eye was equal or inferior to 0.30 logMAR or 0.52 logMAR when recruited from a public hospital or a private clinic, respectively.
notes: q1 Y: best-corrected distance VA in logMAR, correction stated, but chart type/distance not named (could argue U). q2 U: no statement on blinding of VA examiner to questionnaire answers. q3 Y: thresholds stated up front, but they differ by site (0.30 public vs 0.52 private; healthy >=0.10) and are not the conventional low-vision definition; I treated this as Y because they are stated, but it is a judgement call that bears on applicability. q4 U: protocol (chart, distance, eye, testing conditions) not described in detail, though measured prospectively for the study. Incorporation concern: the reference standard defined group membership at enrolment, so sensitivity/specificity describe discrimination of pre-defined groups. Applicability Unclear: VA threshold differs between sites and field, contrast and reading are ignored.

support_quote: The sociodemographic characteristics of the 365 patients who completed the SLVQOL are shown in Table 1 and are classified based on the centre of recruitment, and the visual health status.
notes: q1 U: interval between questionnaire and VA measurement not stated (only stable VA over 6 months before enrolment). q2 Y: all participants had VA, since VA defined the groups. q3 Y: same reference standard (BCVA logMAR) for all, albeit with site-specific thresholds. q4 U: n=365 completed and appear to be all enrolled, but the ROC analysis n is not explicitly stated and missing data are not discussed. Not rated High because no No answers; the only partial concern is that the questionnaire was administered by different modes at the two sites (recorded under D2 q4).

support_quote: Researchers contacted participants from previous studies or patients at each site.
notes: q1 N: participants were contacted from earlier studies or site patients, which is a convenience sample, not consecutive or random. q2 U: this is a single-population design, not two-gate, but recruitment was purposive across the VA spectrum ("no specific requirements for VA") and mean age and VA differ widely by site (Table). q3 N: English-only and the need for existing VA data are inclusion criteria, which excludes non-English speakers (judgement call: it could be read as a minor exclusion). q4 Y: the inclusion criteria (age, VA availability, English) do not depend on survey answers (judgement call: this is inferred from the listed criteria, with no explicit statement). Applicability High: the sample is mostly research-registry and LVR/eye-clinic patients with mean VA 0.58 logMAR, ages 18+ and many diagnoses, so it does not represent a general or primary-care screening population. Fit is poor: this is an IRT estimation study, not a screen with a positive/negative result, so there is no target-condition prevalence.

support_quote: Participants completed the VA survey with an interviewer over the phone or in a clinic at our testing sites.
notes: q1 U: the order and blinding of the survey relative to the VA measurement are not stated. VA came from laboratory, clinic or EHR data, possibly collected long before the survey. q2 NA: there is no positive-screen cut-off, because theta is continuous and mapped to estimated VA by linear regression. This fits poorly (judgement call: the regression equation, 0.59 - 0.33 x theta, was fitted in the same sample, which I counted under q3 rather than q2). q3 N: the 100 items came from iterative development and informal pilot testing. The 2PL model, the linear VA mapping and the accuracy statistics were all fitted and evaluated in the same 385 participants, with no separate development or validation sample, and the authors say refinement is future work. q4 N: administration was by phone or in clinic, was interviewer-led, and took 30-60 min. Mode was not analysed, and the 100-item battery is not a brief screen. Applicability High: a 100-item, 30-60 min interviewer-administered survey is not a brief screening item. Fit is poor: there is no sensitivity or specificity, only correlation (r = -0.73 theta vs VA; r = 0.73 estimated vs measured VA), mean signed and unsigned error (0 and 0.24 logMAR) and the coefficient of repeatability (0.59 logMAR). Note the text gives r = -0.72 in the abstract and -0.73 in the Results; the discrepancy is in the source.

support_quote: The majority of the VA measurements were performed using the Bailey–Lovie or ETDRS charts, except for some measurements using Snellen charts.
notes: q1 U: the charts are standard (Bailey-Lovie, ETDRS, some Snellen), but correction status, eye (better or worse) and distance are not stated. The Discussion says 20-30% may have been Snellen. q2 U: blinding of the VA measurer to survey answers is not stated, and some VA was from existing records, which makes it likely but unconfirmed. q3 NA: no target-condition threshold is defined, because VA is analysed as a continuous variable (the text mentions 0.3 logMAR and 1.0 logMAR only as examples of item thresholds). q4 N: VA came from "laboratory, clinic, or electronic health records" with mixed charts, so there was no single study protocol and the provenance is heterogeneous. Applicability Low (judgement call): measured logMAR VA is an accepted proxy reference for LVR need, but the study gives no LVR-need threshold and ignores field and contrast (contrast sensitivity was only a subset, n = 291).

support_quote: For the purpose of evaluating the development of the survey, the items and participants with poor fits were not excluded in the following analysis.
notes: q1 U: the interval between the survey and the VA measurement is not stated, and VA was pulled from existing data or records. q2 Y: availability of VA data was an inclusion criterion, so all 385 had a reference value (judgement call: this is verification by design, not a stated verification rate). q3 N: three data sources and charts were used (some Snellen; some EHR-derived), which is differential reference standards. The paper acknowledges this itself. q4 Y: all 385 were analysed, including 60 person-misfits and 5 misfit items. The contrast-sensitivity subsets (n = 291 and n = 33) are secondary analyses only. Judgement call: I kept High rather than Unclear because the q3 No and the unknown interval compound across multiple sites. Applicability is NA for this domain.
